narrative:
It's another stereotypical August day today, with patchy morning valley fog burning into a sunny late morning before clouds increase in the afternoon alongside scattered showers and thunderstorms. We had quite a heavy thunderstorm in much of Avery & Watauga yesterday, and localized areas of rain to that extent are possible again this afternoon & evening. Showers become more isolated the first half of this week, before picking back up again.

Real Boone Podcast

I had a great time visiting with Paul and Evan, which resulted in this podcast. I hope you enjoy listening.

2027 Blue Ridge Calendar

The 2027 Blue Ridge Calendar is available online and at retail outlets across the region. Thanks for a record-breaking pre-publication sale! You can see all the winning photography at our Photo Contest page. Check out volume discounts on the calendar and the "Mix and Match" sale on Drinkware.

All Photos Submit Photo Latest Insights July 2026 Recap Holiday Heatwave At the start of the month, there was no relief in sight for the continued dry conditions that the region has been experiencing dating back to the final few months of 2025. July arrived ready to make things worse with what will almost certainly be the heatwave of record for 2026, as record highs abounded throughout the Southern Appalachians for the first handful of days in the month. It felt fitting that America's 250th birthday would coincide with one of the hottest July 4ths on record. Mother Nature seemed to want to celebrate with a bang along with the rest of us. We already wrote extensively about this heatwave a few weeks ago, so if you'd like the full recap, click this link. The quick & dirty version: upper-level ridging and surface high pressure settled over our region, delivering 100s to the Foothills, 90s to the mountains, and 80s to the high elevations. The table below shows recorded highs vs the previous record for each day, with new records highlighted in red, and ties in yellow. Jefferson's 4 consecutive 90F+ highs were all records from the 2nd to the 5th. Beech Mountain does not have an especially long period of record (less than 40 years), but 85F on the 4th is the new highest temperature recorded during that period. The hottest temperatures recorded on our Ray's Weather network of stations throughout this heatwave: 103.0F at Roaring River, 7/3 102.3F at Lenoir, 7/2 102.2F at Morganton-Lenoir Airport, 7/2 & 7/3 100.8F at Hickory, 7/2 96.3F at Asheville, 7/2 93.0F at Boone, 7/2 79.9F at Mount Mitchell, 7/2 (the all-time record is 81F!) Things settled back into a more normal summertime rythym after the heat, with afternoon thunderstorms kicking back up and delivering scattered downpours that began to help some recover their annual rainfall deficit. We'll get deeper into the heavy rains that many experienced in the month of July later on, but the daily graph below shows the story for Celo. Right after the heatwave, over 5 inches of rain fell from the 5th through the 12th, which is pretty close to the average rainfall for the entire month there. One of six days with over an inch of rain in Celo was an abnormally cool July 13th, when 1.47" fell at the foot of the Black Mountains. Further north, stationary showers would make that number pale in comparison. Roaring Gap's Record Rain On the 13th, a cool-air wedge was in place along the eastern side of the Appalachians, and rain showers abounded as moist air was lifted and condensed over the cooler air at the surface. Hickory picked up nearly 2 inches of rain, one of the wettest days of the month there. Along the Eastern Escarpment (an explainer if you need a refresher on the local geography), near where Alleghany, Wilkes, and Surry counties meet, our station at Roaring Gap recorded over 9 inches of rain! Radar estimates nearby exceed 10 inches, and flooding was reported in the area. 9 inches of rain in less than 24 hours will produce flooding anywhere, but fairly dry antecedent conditions likely aided in flooding not being as bad as it could have been. To get such an incredible one-day total, you usually need the help of terrain - which we had in this case. A steady supply of moist air moving up the slope of the escarpment region with little to no "steering" flow to move things around produces stationary showers that can drop localized buckets of rain. A short drive to Mount Airy or eastern Ashe County would have decreased your rainfall amounts as much as tenfold that day! This incredible event, combined with a generally quite wet July, produced a whopping 14.22 inches of rain at Roaing Gap for the month. We'll get into the specifics in the "Precipitation" section further on. A Rare Mountain Tornado A cold front in the summertime usually does not pack much punch, unlike the cold season fronts that put snowflakes and a bitter chill to the air. However, the month of July ended with a couple of abnormally cool mornings, with 40s in the High Country on the 30th. For such an impressive cooldown, you need to bring in a fairly stout front by summer standards, and when you do that, sparks fly. Summer heat and humidity is a powder-keg for storms, and a front adds a focal point to produce more vigorous activity. We got plenty of activity on the 28th! Up in Madison County, just the fifth tornado ever officially surveyed in the county occurred at 5:51PM. It was a weak EF0 tornado, with winds estimated near 80 mph. The track was just 1.1 miles, and the width of the tornado was 75 yards at its widest. The small blue line shows the track below. Damage was "minor and sporadic," limited to broken branches along with a few uprooted and snapped trees. Oddly enough, while there are only 5 surveyed tornadoes on record for Madison Co, 3 of them occurred this year (with two on March 16th). Even outside of the tornado itself, trees were knocked down throughout the county and power outages were common thanks to strong straight-line winds. Our station at Woodson Branch Nature School about 8 or 9 miles northwest of Marshall recorded 2.24 inches of rain before dropping out due to power & internet issues. Temperatures High temperatures were largely fairly close to normal (generally just above it) through the month, with the exceptions being the remarkable heat around the 4th and a couple of cool-air wedge events centered around the 13th and 24th. Those wedges weren't enough for most locations, as highs wound up above normal for most. More of a difference was made in low temperatures, as all of the stations included in the table below were above normal to well above normal on lows. This is thanks to the incredibly humid month we experienced, as moisture and cloud cover do not allow temperatures to drop very much overnight. As a result, it was an above average temperature month region-wide. Specifics lie in the table and map below.

Precipitation July 2026 was about as wet as can be for most. The "percent of normal precip" column does not tell the story as well as the total numbers and the days with precip. Many locations had rain on half or more of the days in July. Celo, Edgemont, Blowing Rock, and Roaring Gap all recorded over 10 inches of rain for the month! Remove Blowing Rock from the grouping, and those 3 stations picked up more than a foot. The vast majority of our stations recieved more than their average rainfall, aside from a few exceptions - notably Jefferson, which the map below the table shows well. Ashe County did not have the rainfall luck that many others did in July. Of the ~60 stations that did not experience outages during July, 38 recorded over 6 inches of rain for the month, and 17 recorded over 8 inches. Amazingly, the area was far enough behind on precipitation for 2026 that techincally, drought conditions do persist for most. However, the level of drought has been reduced notably. But Boone did remained roughly 8 inches "behind schedule" at the end of July (reduced to about 5 inches thanks to heavy rains to start August).

Aug 05, 2026 Monday Message for August 3, 2026 This week's Monday Message discusses the turn to wetter conditions this past weekend and areas of locally torrential rainfall. Also, we look back at a warm and wetter July, while looking forward to more "normal" August weather conditions around WNC and Southwest Virginia. Aug 03, 2026 August 2026 Weather Outlook Forecast Monthly Forecast

Southern Appalachians – SW Virginia & Western North Carolina

August looks like an ordinary month in an extraordinary summer. While Texas and the southern Plains bake under a stubborn ridge, the mountains sit off to the side and finish close to normal — a shade warm overall, a wet first week, and a drier stretch in the middle.

The Typical August: Just Past the Peak

July owns the hottest days of the year, but August gives up little ground — average highs in August run less than 2 degrees cooler than July’s. The retreat is uneven: Hickory sheds 1.7 degrees for its average high in August while Banner Elk gives up only 0.6 degrees, because high elevations cool slowly in late summer. The real break waits until September, which drops five to six degrees below August. This is the last full month of summer, not the first hint of fall.

August is also one of the three wettest months across the mountains, and at Marion, Morganton and North Wilkesboro it is the wettest of all. The reason is the one that makes July wet: by midsummer the fronts that organize our weather have retreated, leaving the terrain in charge. Daytime heating warms the high terrain faster than the free air around it, lifting moist air until it condenses, and afternoon thundershowers repeat day after day. August highs run from 86 degrees at Lenoir down to 66 on Mt Mitchell, a twenty-degree spread within about an hour-and-a-half drive, with lots of climbing!

The Big Picture for August 2026

The dominant feature this month sits a long way from here: a large area of high pressure stretching from the SW U.S. to the Southern Plains — hot, dry, and stubborn. We are east of the heart of the hot air. The heat anomalies will taper as one goes east toward the North Carolina Mountains.

Meanwhile, at least two troughs slide by to our north and northeast during August — one across the Ohio Valley in the first days of the month, another over the Great Lakes near mid-month. Each turns our winds northwesterly for a few days, which in these mountains means somewhat cooler and drier air. Through the first half of the month, the Bermuda High stays mostly offshore, unusual for August and part of why this month will not be a scorcher overall.

The pattern aloft is generally flat all month — no deep trough, no strong ridge in the eastern United States. We sit in the slack middle, between the heat in the Rockies, heat in the Atlantic, and the cooler north. Neither heat nor cool reaches us with much force.

Temperatures: A Cool Start, a Warmer Finish

The month opens cool. A front approaches from the northwest in the first few days, holding temperatures down with clouds and rain. Behind it, high pressure builds over ground wet since mid-July, and damp soil heats slowly — sunshine evaporates water instead of warming air. This may be the only week of the month with below average temperatures.

The second week turns warmer as the western ridge expands east, though the heat arrives much diminished. Near mid-month a trough settles over the Great Lakes, returning us to northwest flow and knocking temperatures back to normal. That cooling is modest. Nothing truly cool exists anywhere in North America in August, so it means lower humidity and a couple of pleasant mornings, not relief. Wytheville, Galax and Sparta feel it most; Asheville and Hendersonville barely at all.

The last ten days warm again as the Bermuda High finally builds westward into the Southeast, putting the month slightly above average — the Foothills more so than the mountains.

Precipitation: A Wet Start, Then a Drier Middle

The front in the first few days may bring the month’s only widespread organized rainfall. After it fades, high pressure and wet ground take over and afternoon thundershowers fire over the terrain day after day — enough for an above average first week. The second week is less wet and warmer in a southwest flow. The third week is driest, as northwest flow behind the mid-month trough brings sinking, drying air and thins thundershower coverage. The last ten days return to near normal, the rain favoring higher terrain.

The surplus is concentrated in the mountains — Celo, Burnsville and Beech Mountain ten to twenty-five percent above normal, Lenoir and Morganton nearer average. Early-month frontal rain falls fairly evenly; the rest depends on afternoon thundershowers, which favor elevation. Because so much of August’s rain is hit-and-miss, two locations a few miles apart can finish an inch and a half apart.

One thing works against a wetter forecast. El Niño is already inhibiting the Atlantic tropical season, its high-altitude winds tearing storms apart before they organize. In an average August the remains of a tropical system can deliver a big total in a hurry — that door looks closed.

Other Items of Note
  • The models agree more closely on temperature than they usually do at this range — European, American and Canadian ensembles all put the mountains within a degree of normal. They agree less on rainfall, specifically on how far west the wet axis sets up. We sit on that boundary, and small shifts in it matter a great deal to the Foothills.
  • As always, this forecast is built from scratch. We work from large-scale model guidance and climate indices (MJO, NAO, AO, and PNA). From that analysis, we reach our own conclusions before looking at anyone else’s forecast. Most of the large-scale indicators in the summer are either non-factors or weak signals. We relied heavily on a blend of long-range models in this forecast. We check the NOAA Climate Prediction Center outlook afterward, for comparison only, never as an input. The NOAA forecast is a little warmer and drier than our forecast.

The Ocean: El Niño Builds Toward Winter

El Niño is firmly established and strengthening. The warmest water sits in the eastern Pacific near the coast of South America, about three degrees Celsius above normal, tapering westward to near normal at the International Date Line. That geography matters: events with the warmth concentrated toward the eastern Pacific produce the textbook winter response over North America, and this one is about as east-focused as they come. The two graphs below show the current Sea Surface Temperature Anomalies globally and the forecast for the strength of the El Niño in the coming months.

The atmosphere is catching up with the ocean now, which is the sign forecasters look for. Thunderstorm activity that normally sits over Indonesia has shifted thousands of miles east into the central Pacific, and the winds aloft have reorganized to match. That coupling is what lets a warm patch of tropical ocean rearrange weather over North America months later. This will be a very strong El Niño. It peaks in late autumn, holds through early winter, and slowly fades early next year.

Look also at the cooler than average water in the Gulf of Guinea, off West Africa — sometimes called an Atlantic Niña. We flagged it last month, and it has deepened rather than faded. Along with El Niño’s high-altitude winds, it is one more factor working against Atlantic tropical development this season.

The other ocean story is broader: most of the world’s oceans are running warm. The subtropical North Atlantic set record temperatures four months running this spring, and by June roughly eighty-two percent of the global ocean was in a marine heatwave — the second largest extent ever measured. Warmer water puts more moisture into the air, and for us that shows up first in overnight lows. Cool nights are this region’s signature — Jefferson averages a low of 57 in August, Mt Mitchell 51 — and they depend on air dry enough to radiate heat away after sunset. Higher humidity results in warmer low temperatures and means heavier downpours when storms do form.

What would that mean for winter? If this El Niño behaves the way most of them do, the Southern Appalachians finish wetter than normal, with the storm track running along the Gulf Coast and up the East Coast and delivering more systems than an average winter. The record of El Niño winters going back to 1950 shows above-average snowfall across the southern Appalachians.

The catch is that these are typically not very cold winters. What produces the snow is storm frequency and elevation rather than deep cold — the same system that gives Banner Elk and Beech Mountain a foot can give Hickory a cold rain. (This does NOT mean that the Foothills will be without snow or ice this winter.) Expect a busy winter in the Southern Appalachians — with a variety of precipitation types.

We will have much more to say about all of this in the RaysWeather.com Fearless Forecast for Winter 2026/27 that is published in the 3rd week of October.

The small blue line shows the track below.; Damage was "minor and sporadic," limited to broken branches along with a few uprooted and snapped trees. Oddly enough, while there are only 5 surveyed tornadoes on record for Madison Co, 3 of them occurred this year (with two on March 16th). Even outside of the tornado itself, trees were knocked down throughout the county and power outages were common thanks to strong straight-line winds. Our station at Woodson Branch Nature School about 8 or 9 miles northwest of Marshall recorded 2.24 inches of rain before dropping out due to power & internet issues.; Temperatures; High temperatures were largely fairly close to normal (generally just above it) through the month, with the exceptions being the remarkable heat around the 4th and a couple of cool-air wedge events centered around the 13th and 24th. Those wedges weren't enough for most locations, as highs wound up above normal for most. More of a difference was made in low temperatures, as all of the stations included in the table below were above normal to well above normal on lows. This is thanks to the incredibly humid month we experienced, as moisture and cloud cover do not allow temperatures to drop very much overnight.; As a result, it was an above average temperature month region-wide. Also, we look back at a warm and wetter July, while looking forward to more "normal" August weather conditions around WNC and Southwest Virginia.; Aug 03, 2026; August 2026 Weather Outlook; Forecast; Monthly Forecast;

Southern Appalachians – SW Virginia & Western North Carolina

August looks like an ordinary month in an extraordinary summer. While Texas and the southern Plains bake under a stubborn ridge, the mountains sit off to the side and finish close to normal — a shade warm overall, a wet first week, and a drier stretch in the middle.

; The Typical August: Just Past the Peak;

July owns the hottest days of the year, but August gives up little ground — average highs in August run less than 2 degrees cooler than July’s. The retreat is uneven: Hickory sheds 1.7 degrees for its average high in August while Banner Elk gives up only 0.6 degrees, because high elevations cool slowly in late summer. The real break waits until September, which drops five to six degrees below August. This is the last full month of summer, not the first hint of fall.

August is also one of the three wettest months across the mountains, and at Marion, Morganton and North Wilkesboro it is the wettest of all. The reason is the one that makes July wet: by midsummer the fronts that organize our weather have retreated, leaving the terrain in charge. Daytime heating warms the high terrain faster than the free air around it, lifting moist air until it condenses, and afternoon thundershowers repeat day after day. August highs run from 86 degrees at Lenoir down to 66 on Mt Mitchell, a twenty-degree spread within about an hour-and-a-half drive, with lots of climbing!

; The Big Picture for August 2026;

The dominant feature this month sits a long way from here: a large area of high pressure stretching from the SW U.S. to the Southern Plains — hot, dry, and stubborn. We are east of the heart of the hot air. The heat anomalies will taper as one goes east toward the North Carolina Mountains.

Meanwhile, at least two troughs slide by to our north and northeast during August — one across the Ohio Valley in the first days of the month, another over the Great Lakes near mid-month. Each turns our winds northwesterly for a few days, which in these mountains means somewhat cooler and drier air. Through the first half of the month, the Bermuda High stays mostly offshore, unusual for August and part of why this month will not be a scorcher overall.

The pattern aloft is generally flat all month — no deep trough, no strong ridge in the eastern United States. We sit in the slack middle, between the heat in the Rockies, heat in the Atlantic, and the cooler north. Neither heat nor cool reaches us with much force.

; Temperatures: A Cool Start, a Warmer Finish;

The month opens cool. A front approaches from the northwest in the first few days, holding temperatures down with clouds and rain. Behind it, high pressure builds over ground wet since mid-July, and damp soil heats slowly — sunshine evaporates water instead of warming air. This may be the only week of the month with below average temperatures.

The second week turns warmer as the western ridge expands east, though the heat arrives much diminished. Near mid-month a trough settles over the Great Lakes, returning us to northwest flow and knocking temperatures back to normal. That cooling is modest. Nothing truly cool exists anywhere in North America in August, so it means lower humidity and a couple of pleasant mornings, not relief. Wytheville, Galax and Sparta feel it most; Asheville and Hendersonville barely at all.

The last ten days warm again as the Bermuda High finally builds westward into the Southeast, putting the month slightly above average — the Foothills more so than the mountains.

; Precipitation: A Wet Start, Then a Drier Middle;

The front in the first few days may bring the month’s only widespread organized rainfall. After it fades, high pressure and wet ground take over and afternoon thundershowers fire over the terrain day after day — enough for an above average first week. The second week is less wet and warmer in a southwest flow. The third week is driest, as northwest flow behind the mid-month trough brings sinking, drying air and thins thundershower coverage. The last ten days return to near normal, the rain favoring higher terrain.

The surplus is concentrated in the mountains — Celo, Burnsville and Beech Mountain ten to twenty-five percent above normal, Lenoir and Morganton nearer average. Early-month frontal rain falls fairly evenly; the rest depends on afternoon thundershowers, which favor elevation. Because so much of August’s rain is hit-and-miss, two locations a few miles apart can finish an inch and a half apart.

One thing works against a wetter forecast. El Niño is already inhibiting the Atlantic tropical season, its high-altitude winds tearing storms apart before they organize. In an average August the remains of a tropical system can deliver a big total in a hurry — that door looks closed.

; The Ocean: El Niño Builds Toward Winter;

El Niño is firmly established and strengthening. The warmest water sits in the eastern Pacific near the coast of South America, about three degrees Celsius above normal, tapering westward to near normal at the International Date Line. That geography matters: events with the warmth concentrated toward the eastern Pacific produce the textbook winter response over North America, and this one is about as east-focused as they come. The two graphs below show the current Sea Surface Temperature Anomalies globally and the forecast for the strength of the El Niño in the coming months.

;

The atmosphere is catching up with the ocean now, which is the sign forecasters look for. Thunderstorm activity that normally sits over Indonesia has shifted thousands of miles east into the central Pacific, and the winds aloft have reorganized to match. That coupling is what lets a warm patch of tropical ocean rearrange weather over North America months later. This will be a very strong El Niño. It peaks in late autumn, holds through early winter, and slowly fades early next year.

Look also at the cooler than average water in the Gulf of Guinea, off West Africa — sometimes called an Atlantic Niña. We flagged it last month, and it has deepened rather than faded. Along with El Niño’s high-altitude winds, it is one more factor working against Atlantic tropical development this season.

The other ocean story is broader: most of the world’s oceans are running warm. The subtropical North Atlantic set record temperatures four months running this spring, and by June roughly eighty-two percent of the global ocean was in a marine heatwave — the second largest extent ever measured. Warmer water puts more moisture into the air, and for us that shows up first in overnight lows. Cool nights are this region’s signature — Jefferson averages a low of 57 in August, Mt Mitchell 51 — and they depend on air dry enough to radiate heat away after sunset. Higher humidity results in warmer low temperatures and means heavier downpours when storms do form.

What would that mean for winter? If this El Niño behaves the way most of them do, the Southern Appalachians finish wetter than normal, with the storm track running along the Gulf Coast and up the East Coast and delivering more systems than an average winter. The record of El Niño winters going back to 1950 shows above-average snowfall across the southern Appalachians.

The catch is that these are typically not very cold winters. What produces the snow is storm frequency and elevation rather than deep cold — the same system that gives Banner Elk and Beech Mountain a foot can give Hickory a cold rain. (This does NOT mean that the Foothills will be without snow or ice this winter.) Expect a busy winter in the Southern Appalachians — with a variety of precipitation types.

We will have much more to say about all of this in the RaysWeather.com Fearless Forecast for Winter 2026/27 that is published in the 3rd week of October.
